p: Nobody wants to spend half of their session stood at a desk, so a little prep goes a long way. Each climber will need a participation form completing, with a parent or guardian signing for anyone under 18. Most people find it easiest to do this online the night before. It's also worth reading the age guidance when you book, as there's normally a minimum age and some supervision rules for younger children.

Give the whole visit a couple of hours. That covers turning up a bit early, getting harnessed, the safety briefing and the climb itself, without anyone feeling rushed. Wear trainers and clothes that let you lift your knees high, tie back long hair and pop a water bottle in the bag.

If you've got a nervous climber in the group, try this: let them do a low climb and let go after only a metre or so. Feeling how softly the auto-belay lowers you takes away most of the fear. Then it's a case of going a little higher each time, and they'll be at the top before long.

For later, the University Botanic Garden is a peaceful, beautifully kept spot just south of the centre, while the riverside walk across the meadows to Grantchester is a Cambridge classic, ending with a cuppa in the village. If the weather turns, the Grand Arcade and the Lion Yard shops are right in the middle of town.
